name: Achterberg Pollinator Ecology Lab — faculty desktop transfer (SYNTHETIC)
source: Full copy of the office desktop computer of Professor Miriam K. Achterberg, transferred by departmental IT on her retirement in June 2024. Includes the user profile (Desktop, Documents, Downloads, Pictures, Music), an exported mailbox, a lab external drive copied into the profile, and a backup folder from her previous computer (2004-2009). Nothing was selected or weeded before transfer; the drive is as she left it.
owner: Miriam K. Achterberg, Professor Emerita of Entomology, Department of Entomology. Donor agreement on file with the Archives (reference DA-2024-117, synthetic).
role: Assistant Professor 2006, Associate Professor 2012, Professor 2018, retired 2024. Director of the Achterberg Pollinator Ecology Lab 2006-2024. Lead PI of NSF DEB-1900417 (2019-2023). Advised 6 PhD and 9 MS students.
scope: Faculty research, teaching and service records, 2004-2024, with the bulk dating 2015-2023. The research centres on the Prairie Bee Survey, a long-term study of native bee communities on ten restored and remnant tallgrass prairie sites in east-central Illinois.
research: Field ecology and conservation biology: pan-trap and net surveys of wild bees, specimen identification and DNA barcoding, floral resource surveys, statistical modelling of community recovery after prairie restoration, GIS mapping of survey sites, and outreach with state natural-areas staff and private landowners.
bio: Achterberg's lab produced the most cited demonstration that native bee species richness recovers within roughly a decade of prairie restoration while ground-nesting specialist bees lag far behind. The survey's 2019-2022 data include the only recent records of the federally endangered rusty patched bumble bee (Bombus affinis) in Ford County. She worked closely with statistician Rafael Quintero (Prairie State University) and with Illinois DNR natural-areas staff, and her graduate students Priya Natarajan and Jonah Feld carried out most fieldwork from 2018.
valuable: Original research data from the Prairie Bee Survey, including raw pan-trap and netting records, specimen databases, floral surveys and site metadata. Field notebooks, field photographs of the survey sites, and photographs or images of bee specimens. Analysis code, scripts and notebooks that produced the published results, and the figures they generated. Drafts of manuscripts, reviewer correspondence and response letters that show how the papers changed, including dissertation chapters she supervised. Grant proposals, progress reports and data-management plans for the NSF award and related funding. Correspondence with collaborators, students, Illinois DNR staff and landowners that discusses methods, findings, site access or conservation decisions. GIS layers and maps of survey sites. Recordings, slides and talks presenting the research, and oral-history or interview material about the history of the sites. Her own annotated copies of literature, where her notes show how she used the source. Her curriculum vitae and records documenting her career and the lab's history.
exclude: Operating-system files, application caches, installers and software downloads. Exact duplicates of files kept elsewhere in the transfer. Personal financial, tax, medical and household records unrelated to her university work. Family photographs and personal media such as music libraries. Routine departmental announcements, building notices, parking and IT messages that she did not write. Vendor marketing, newsletters she only subscribed to, spam and phishing messages. Unannotated copies of published articles by other authors that are available from the publisher. Routine course administration such as rosters, gradebooks and travel booking confirmations, beyond one representative syllabus per course.
access: The survey contains precise locations of rusty patched bumble bee colonies on private land; exact coordinates for the Ritter Farm Remnant (site BRF) must not appear in any open-web release and should be generalised to county. Student records (grades, applications, letters about students) are FERPA-protected. Personnel matters concerning lab staff, medical leave documentation, and any Social Security numbers or banking details must be restricted. Peer reviews she wrote of other authors' unpublished manuscripts are confidential. Any credentials or passwords found must be flagged and never published.
notes: SYNTHETIC TEST ACCESSION. Every person, site, identifier and record in this transfer is invented for pipeline validation. Ground-truth labels live in labels/ and must never be passed to the pipeline under test.
